meta.tagline: A romantic fairytale in the palaces of a misty mountain

pills: Next door to Europe's westernmost point

overview.title: Welcome to Sintra
overview.intro: Sintra is not a town but a state of mind: Atlantic mist winds through the mountain forests, ivy swallows the walls, and on every hilltop stands another dreamer's palace. Red-and-yellow-towered Pena floats above the clouds, the steps of Regaleira's well spiral into the earth, and the Moorish ramparts wander the ridges. Lord Byron called this place a 'glorious Eden', and he wasn't wrong. But even Eden has its rules: come early, go slowly, and treat the mist as scenery, not a flaw.

local_word.definition: The short name of the Sintra Mountains: when someone says 'the serra' they mean the forested granite mass that wraps the town. It makes its own microclimate — the serra can be misty while Lisbon basks in sun. For locals it isn't weather, it's character.

rules.title: Come early, go against the current
rules.description: Sintra is Lisbon's favourite day trip: the crowds arrive at 10.30. Take the first train, and while everyone runs to Pena, start at Regaleira — or do exactly the opposite. Whoever swims against the current sees the palaces empty.

rules.title: Buy timed palace tickets in advance
rules.description: Pena Palace runs on timed tickets, and on summer days the ticket office sells out. Choose two, at most three sights — whoever tries to cram them all into one day ends up truly seeing none.

rules.title: Forget the car — trust your feet and the bus
rules.description: The mountain roads are narrow, parking impossible, the tow truck merciless. Come by train; use buses 434 (Pena) and 435 (Regaleira-Monserrate) or the walking trails — the forest paths are the best part of the visit anyway.

quick_facts.label: Language
quick_facts.sub: English common on the tourist trail

tip.label: The Sintra philosophy
tip.text: In Sintra the mist is not your enemy but the stage manager: as Pena slips in and out of cloud, the fairytale factor rises. Those after guaranteed sun can wait for noon; those after atmosphere should run to the morning mist.

transport.title: Getting Around
transport.intro: Train to Sintra, bus and feet within it: break this three-part rule and you'll spend your day hunting for parking.

items.title: The train from Lisbon
items.description: A train every 20-30 minutes from Rossio station reaches Sintra in 40: load a Viva Viagem card and tap through. The first morning trains are the only way to beat the crowd.

items.title: 434 — the Pena loop
items.description: The 434 from the station loops through the historic centre, the Moorish Castle and Pena and back: it runs one-way, and the day ticket makes sense. The queue is shortest early in the morning.

items.title: 435 — the valley line
items.description: The 435 to Regaleira, Seteais and Monserrate runs independently of the Pena crowds: the comfortable way to the valley's quieter palaces.

items.title: The forest paths
items.description: Ten minutes from the centre to Regaleira, or a 45-minute forest climb to Pena via the Vila Sassetti path: walking among ferns, giant sequoias and mist beats the bus. Trying it downhill is kinder to the knees.

items.title: The Cabo da Roca connection
items.description: The coastal bus from the station reaches Cabo da Roca, Europe's westernmost point, in 40 minutes: the Sintra + ocean's-edge combination is the same day's best second act.

callout.label: Route tip
callout.text: The crowds are beaten by reverse logic: at opening enter Regaleira instead of Pena (it's nearly empty at the door), and visit Pena after 3.30 pm on a timed ticket — the tour buses are on the road back to Lisbon by then.

stay.title: Where to Stay
stay.intro: The day-trippers ride the evening train home; those who stay see the real Sintra — the one where the mist settles and the palaces fall silent.

local_word.definition: A manor house or estate with gardens: Sintra's slopes are full of 19th-century aristocrats' quintas. Most are boutique hotels now — waking up in an ivy-clad quinta is the full dose of Sintra romance.

items.name: The historic centre (Vila)
items.description: The narrow lanes at the foot of the National Palace's chimneys: bakery smells, azulejo façades and the fairytale silence that falls in the evening. Crowded by day, entirely yours at night.

items.name: São Pedro de Penaferrim
items.description: The calm quarter above the centre: antique dealers, family restaurants, and the historic fair held on the month's second and fourth Sundays. Real town life outside the tourist wave.

items.name: The hillside quintas
items.description: Historic manor hotels hidden in the forest: ivy-hung gardens, fountained courtyards, breakfasts with a view of the mist. The option that turns Sintra's soul into lodging — a honeymoon classic.

items.name: Colares
items.description: The wine village on the mountain's seaward foot: Colares wine, from some of the world's oldest sand-grown vines, is born here. Rental houses and rural calm — a coast + palace balance for those with a car.

items.name: Praia das Maçãs and Azenhas do Mar
items.description: Sintra's beach villages: white houses spilling down a cliff, an ocean pool and fish restaurants. In summer the historic tram links to the centre — palace mornings, ocean evenings.

best_time.title: When to Go
best_time.intro: In the serra's microclimate all four seasons can happen in one day; the real choice is made by the crowd calendar.

items.label: Spring
items.name: Camellias and Dancing Mist
items.subtitle: Spring · Flowering gardens, fresh green
items.description: The gardens open with camellias and magnolias, the forest turns its brightest green, and the air is walking-cool. Crowds below summer levels — Sintra's most balanced season.

callout.label: May tip
callout.text: In May the Monserrate gardens peak: fern valleys, the rose garden and nearly empty paths. In defiance of Pena's queue, give this place the longest hour of your day.

items.label: Summer
items.name: Peak Crowds, Cool Mountain
items.subtitle: Summer · Escape from Lisbon's heat, full capacity
items.description: While Lisbon roasts, the serra runs 5-8 degrees cooler: which is why everyone is here. The palaces fill even on timed tickets and the 434 queue stretches. The come-early-stay-late strategy and a beach escape are summer's keys.

callout.label: August note
callout.text: In August don't go near Pena between 10.30 and 15.30: book the first slot or the last. Give midday to Cabo da Roca and Praia das Maçãs — the ocean wind knows no queue.

items.label: Autumn
items.name: The Golden Forest
items.subtitle: Autumn · Soft light, receding crowds
items.description: September is still summer, but with October the forest turns to copper, the mist takes the stage more often and the palaces can breathe. The season of photographers and slow travellers.

callout.label: October tip
callout.text: On a misty October morning climb the Moorish Castle: the ramparts vanish and reappear in the cloud, and Pena glides past like a ghost. A misty day isn't 'bad weather' — it's Sintra's best filter.

items.label: Winter
items.name: Misty Tale, Empty Palaces
items.subtitle: Winter · Rain breaks, romance without tourists
items.description: Rain and mist wrap the serra, the palaces nearly empty, and the fireplace quintas become the season's stars. Whoever minds the wet stone sees Sintra as Byron saw it.

callout.label: January tip
callout.text: On a winter weekday you'll find Pena tickets even at the gate, and the terraces are left to you: wait out the rain, shoot as the mist lifts — the frames that exist on no postcard appear in that moment.

eat.title: What to Eat
eat.intro: Sintra's cooking begins at the pastry counter: two legendary sweets are the town bakeries' pride; the mountain villages and the ocean complete the rest.

local_word.definition: 'Pillow': the Sintra classic of puff pastry rolled around almond cream and dusted with sugar. Served warm and gone in two bites — the queue outside the town's most famous bakery exists for this pillow.

items.name: Travesseiro — the warm pillow
items.description: An almond-cream puff roll at the moment it leaves the oven: crisp outside, warm inside. The classic of the Piriquita bakery — if the queue is long, know that a fresh tray has just come out.
items.tag: Served warm · a queue is a good sign

items.name: Queijada de Sintra
items.description: A fresh-cheese-and-cinnamon tart in thin crisp pastry: a miniature legend made since the 13th century and sold in paper rolls of half a dozen. A comparative tasting against the travesseiro is compulsory.
items.tag: A centuries-old recipe · buy half a dozen

items.name: Ocean fish at Azenhas do Mar
items.description: The day's fish and shellfish in the cliff village's restaurants: the sound of waves and the view of the ocean pool are included. The finest cure for palace fatigue.
items.tag: In the coastal village · the day's catch

items.name: Leitão and the mountain table
items.description: The surrounding villages' roast suckling pig (leitão) and ember-grilled chouriço are weekend-table classics: at São Pedro's family restaurants, with generous sides. Filling, honest, local.
items.tag: In São Pedro's restaurants · at the weekend

items.name: Colares wine
items.description: A rare wine from century-old vines that survived the phylloxera plague in sand: the Ramisco red with its salty Atlantic character. Little is made and it's hard to find — try it by the glass wherever you see it.
items.tag: A rarity · from the sand vineyards

items.name: A ginjinha pause and a bica
items.description: Sour-cherry liqueur (ginjinha) in a tiny glass, an espresso (bica) beside it: the Portuguese mid-sightseeing break in summary. Ginjinha in a chocolate cup is touristy, but a sweet game.
items.tag: Between sights · in a tiny glass

callout.label: The bakery rule
callout.text: Don't have your travesseiro boxed to go — eat it warm at the counter: this pastry does not travel. Don't let the queue scare you; the trays are replenished constantly and the line moves faster than it looks.

hidden_gems.title: Hidden Corners
hidden_gems.intro: Everyone sees Pena; these six are what Sintra hides behind the mist.

items.rarity: A tower descending into the earth
items.name: Regaleira's Initiation Well
items.description: The inverted tower of Quinta da Regaleira: a 27-metre spiral staircase sinks into the ground and connects at the bottom through cave tunnels to a waterfall. With its Masonic symbols and mossy stones, this is Sintra's mystery in distilled form. Enter at the first hour — catching the well empty is possible.

items.name: The Moorish Castle mist watch
items.description: The 9th-century walls ripple along the mountain's spine: on a clear day you look to the Atlantic, on a misty one over a sea of cloud. The crowds queuing for Pena rarely detour here — the rampart walk is usually calm.

items.name: Monserrate Palace
items.description: Around the Indo-Gothic domed palace, the world's plants spill down the valley: fern glens, a Mexican garden, a rose valley. Sintra's least crowded, most underrated jewel — it deserves half a day.

items.name: Convento dos Capuchos
items.description: A 16th-century friars' convent of cork-lined cells deep in the forest: the exact opposite of Pena's splendour — stone and silence. This is what people mean by 'Sintra's other face'.

items.rarity: A path through a palace garden
items.name: The Vila Sassetti path
items.description: The stone-laid forest path from the centre up towards Pena passes through the garden of an Italianate villa: sequoias, fountains and birdsong. The most graceful alternative to the 434 queue — beautiful downhill too.

items.rarity: The white village on the cliff
items.name: Azenhas do Mar
items.description: White houses pouring down an ocean cliff and a sea pool carved into the rocks: the village that washes away ticket fatigue with salt air. Look from the viewpoint above at sunset — the postcard takes itself.

callout.label: Path tip
callout.text: Sintra's paths are as much heritage as its palaces: link the Regaleira-Seteais-Monserrate line on foot and collect the fountains and gateways that drivers never see. The forest shade stays cool even in summer — a water bottle is enough.

traps.title: Tourist Traps
traps.intro: Sintra's trap is not bad faith but crowd arithmetic: knowledge of hours and order changes everything.

items.name: Arriving unplanned and trying to see everything
items.description: Whoever tries to fit five palaces + the castle + the gardens into one day finishes it in queues and buses, savouring none of it.
items.instead: Choose two sights and count a third as bonus: the classic pair is Pena + Regaleira, the quiet pair Monserrate + Capuchos. Buy timed tickets online and link the gaps with paths.

items.name: Driving your own car up the mountain
items.description: The mountain road is narrow and one-way, parking close to nonexistent; a wrong park introduces you to the tow truck.
items.instead: Come by train and move by 434/435 and the paths. If you did drive, leave the car near the station or in the car parks at the town's entrance — never go up.

items.name: Tuk-tuk haggling outside the station
items.description: The tuk-tuks offering a 'private tour to Pena' ask ten times the bus fare; the road is the same road, the queue the same queue.
items.instead: Buy the 434 day ticket or walk the Vila Sassetti path. If you fancy a tuk-tuk, use it where the bus doesn't go — a Colares-Azenhas coastal run — with the price fixed first.

items.name: Entering Pena's state rooms at noon
items.description: Even with timed tickets, in the midday slots you shuffle step by step through the palace corridors, and the terraces become a selfie stage.
items.instead: Book the first slot or after 3.30 pm; if you're stuck with midday, do the park and terraces first and leave the state rooms for the slot's second half.

callout.label: Golden rule
callout.text: In Sintra the hour matters more than the place: the second-choice palace at the right hour gives more than Pena at the wrong one. And remember — for those who stay, evening Sintra is a different town the day-trippers never meet.

itinerary.title: Ready-Made Routes
itinerary.intro: If you hate planning, follow these flows. The times are flexible; keep the spirit, break the order.

plans.title: If You Have 1 Day
plans.subtitle: From the well to the palace, against the current

steps.title: First train + Regaleira
steps.description: Catch one of the first trains from Rossio; walk from the station and enter Regaleira at opening. Go straight to the Initiation Well — the first half hour is nearly empty.

steps.title: Up the Vila Sassetti path
steps.description: Climb towards Pena on the stone path through the forest: sequoias, mist and birdsong. A breather on the ramparts of the Moorish Castle.

steps.title: Lunch in town + the sweet duel
steps.description: A light lunch in the centre, then the comparative tasting of travesseiro versus queijada: you declare the winner.

steps.title: Pena Palace — the late slot
steps.description: Into the coloured palace on a timed ticket: with the tour buses on their way home, the terraces relax. The park viewpoints first, then the state rooms.

steps.title: The National Palace and its chimneys
steps.description: Evening light on the white-chimneyed palace on the town square: go inside, or watch the façade from a square café.

steps.title: Evening Sintra
steps.description: When the day-trippers board the train, the town is yours: an evening walk through ivy-hung lanes, a local table in São Pedro — the tale's quiet finale.

plans.title: If You Have 3 Days
plans.subtitle: Palaces, mist and ocean — the full Sintra

steps.title: Classic Sintra
steps.description: The one-day flow above: Regaleira, the path, the castle, Pena, the town evening.

steps.title: The quiet palaces day
steps.description: A long morning in the Monserrate gardens; the silence of the Capuchos convent in the afternoon; wine in a quinta garden in the evening — don't forget to have a bottle of Colares opened.

steps.title: The ocean's edge and farewell
steps.description: The coastal bus to the continent's-edge wind at Cabo da Roca; fish at Azenhas do Mar for lunch; the ocean pool at Praia das Maçãs on the way back — seal the palace fairytale with salt water.

phrases.title: 5-Word Survival Kit
phrases.intro: Portuguese is a courteous language; these five carry you from the pastry counter to the palace gate.

items.meaning: Good morning — the opening greeting of the bakery queue
Thank you — ends in -o if you're male, -a if you're female
Please — 'um travesseiro, por favor' is the day's most important sentence
'How beautiful!' — it will escape you unbidden on Pena's terrace
Cheers! — as the Colares glass rises

checklist.title: Sintra Checklist
checklist.completion_message: Que lindo! You've lived the misty fairytale properly!
